clue.text: Here I am with a problem in arithmetic

definitions.meaning: the Latin word a pupil answers at a roll call, meaning 'present'
read as 'add sum', an exercise in addition

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition works by sound: split the Latin word and it sounds like 'add sum', the kind of problem a schoolchild does in arithmetic.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin roll-call response means 'I am present', and its two syllables also say 'add sum', a classroom exercise.

clue.text: Lofty, the Greek sailor, such a wit

parts.note: attic means at the top of a house, lofty, and also Athenian, Greek
an old salt is a sailor

explanation.surface: A tall Greek seaman is a famous joker.
explanation.walkthrough: Attic does double duty: a loft, and Athenian, as in the Greek region of Attica.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names refined, elegant wit of the kind the Athenians were famed for.

clue.text: Direction not very good on the track

parts.note: S is south, a compass direction
poor means not very good

explanation.surface: A runner is told his heading on the circuit is not much good.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunters follow the trail or droppings an animal leaves, its trail.

clue.text: A flower in my upper hand

indicators.note: one piece is put in the other, inside its letters

parts.note: an aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: A gardener holds a bloom up in his raised hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Having the upper hand means being in control, which is command or dominance.

clue.text: There's no punctuality when one feeds among sailors

indicators.note: one piece sits among the letters of the other, so it goes inside

parts.note: tars is an old word for sailors
someone who feeds dines

explanation.surface: Meal times aboard ship are never kept to the clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Lateness is the absence of punctuality, so where it reigns there is none.

clue.text: Saving grace of the endless break

indicators.note: endless means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a rift is a break or split

explanation.surface: A small redeeming feature of an otherwise never-ending holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' cuts the last letter of THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Frugality is the virtue of saving money, a grace of good housekeeping.

clue.text: Among engineers I clear up with the weapon of satire

indicators.note: the pieces go among the letters of the engineers, inside them

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: lucid means clear

explanation.surface: An engineer explains himself clearly while being mocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' reverses the synonym for 'clear' because this is a down clue; the Royal Engineers are a British army corps, and the page prints 'I' that the feed lost.
explanation.definitionFit: Mockery is the satirist's chief weapon, making a target laughable.

clue.text: One born out of five it seems has been asked in

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: out of says one piece lies outside the other, around it

parts.note: nee means born, as in a maiden name
V is the Roman numeral five
taken as written

explanation.surface: A single child out of quintuplets seems to have been invited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of' is read as 'outside': the word for 'born' wraps the five and 'it'; 'seems' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A guest is someone who has received an invitation to come in.

clue.text: In trading centres the unknown quantity sounds variable

indicators.note: sounds says the letter is to be heard, not written

parts.note: x is the algebraist's unknown quantity
something variable changes

explanation.surface: A trader in the markets finds his unknown figure keeps shifting.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter X said aloud is 'ex'; in algebra x is the unknown that varies.
explanation.definitionFit: Stock and commodity markets are buildings where trading goes on.

clue.text: This violin can be played upside down

indicators.note: in a down clue upside down means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: darts is a game, something that can be played

explanation.surface: A fiddle that can be played even when held the wrong way up.
explanation.walkthrough: The game played, DARTS, written upside down gives the violin's short name, after Stradivarius.
explanation.definitionFit: A short name for a violin made by Antonio Stradivari.

clue.text: In the bags

parts.note: bags is British slang for trousers, so someone in bags is wearing them; the phrase also hints at something pocketed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bags' looks like luggage or sacks, but in British slang it means a pair of trousers, so being in them describes someone dressed in that garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A person wearing trousers is described with this adjective, and bags are loose trousers.

clue.text: One who, like Dr. Primrose, takes an age getting home

definitions.text: One who, like Dr. Primrose, takes an age getting home

parts.words: One who, like Dr. Primrose, takes an age getting home
parts.note: Dr Primrose is the clergyman hero of Goldsmith's novel set in Wakefield; add the word 'age' to his title and you get the name of the house a parish priest lives in

explanation.surface: A slow traveller dawdles on the way back, like a character from an old novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Dr Primrose is the hero of Oliver Goldsmith's 'The Vicar of Wakefield'. Tack AGE on to his job title and it becomes VICARAGE, his home, which is what 'takes an age getting home' describes.
explanation.definitionFit: Goldsmith's Dr Primrose is a parish clergyman, and such a cleric's house is named by adding 'age' to his title.

clue.text: A square of diamonds that's anathema to Sandy

definitions.meaning: nine is three squared, so the nine of diamonds is a square number of that suit
Sandy is a stock name for a Scotsman, so a thing he curses is a bane of Scotland

explanation.walkthrough: The nine of diamonds is traditionally called this; 'square' is there because nine is a square number. Sandy is a nickname for a Scot.
explanation.definitionFit: The traditional nickname for the nine of diamonds playing card names it as a national bane for Scots.

clue.text: Reduces? Carried unanimously (almost)

indicators.note: the phrase is not quite given in full, so one letter has to go

parts.note: a motion carried unanimously gets all ayes in the vote

explanation.surface: A motion to cut costs passes without a dissenting voice, or nearly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' drops the E from ALL AYES, a unanimous vote, leaving a word that also sounds nearly the same.
explanation.definitionFit: To lessen a fear or pain is to reduce it, which is what calming or soothing does.

clue.text: On the farm they tend to be so rural

definitions.text: On the farm they tend to be so rural

indicators.note: tend to here hints that the letters are inclined to wander into a new order

explanation.surface: Farmhands are country folk by nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tend to' rearranges BE SO RURAL; read whole, the clue says farmhands who tend crops are apt to be rustic.
explanation.definitionFit: Hired farmhands tend the fields and livestock, and their work is rustic.

clue.text: Reacting abnormally and with unusually ill grace

indicators.note: unusually signals that these letters appear in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Someone responds out of the ordinary and with very bad manners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusually' rearranges ILL GRACE.
explanation.definitionFit: An immune system that overreacts to pollen or nuts produces a hypersensitive response.

clue.text: Ends instruction to puzzlers without a penny

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: con clues: con means study, so the phrase tells solvers what to do
d was the abbreviation for a penny in old British money

explanation.surface: The instructions to solvers finish with a note that entry is free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' means outside here: CON CLUES around D, the old British penny.
explanation.definitionFit: To end something is to bring it to a close or finish it.

clue.text: Programme for better types

parts.note: better here means one who bets; the printed list of horses and times sold at a meeting is for them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Better types' looks like superior people, but a better is someone who places bets, and this programme lists the runners at a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Punters at a horse-racing meeting buy a printed programme listing the races and runners.

clue.text: Slipshod conveyance

parts.note: slipshod usually means careless, but here it means shod for slipping: a vehicle on runners that slides over snow

explanation.walkthrough: 'Slipshod' looks like 'sloppy', but it is read literally: a vehicle whose feet are made for slipping along.
explanation.definitionFit: A sled for sliding down snowy slopes is a vehicle fitted with runners for slipping.

clue.text: Its safety-pin adds point to danger perhaps

definitions.text: Its safety-pin adds point to danger perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters could be in some other order

parts.note: E is east, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A bomb's pin makes the threat sharper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adds point to' puts E (east, a compass point) with DANGER, and 'perhaps' shuffles them; read whole, a pulled pin sharpens danger.
explanation.definitionFit: A hand-thrown bomb has a safety pin pulled before it is thrown.

clue.text: A prayer for Bob in the hunter's clutches

indicators.note: one piece sits in the grip of the other, so it goes inside
clutches pairs with 'in' to say the hunter holds this piece

parts.note: Orion is the hunter of Greek myth and the constellation
a bob was a shilling in old British money, abbreviated s

explanation.surface: A hunted man named Bob says a prayer while caught by his pursuer.
explanation.walkthrough: A bob was a shilling in pre-decimal British money, written s; Orion is the hunter.
explanation.definitionFit: An old literary word for a prayer, used by Shakespeare and others.

clue.text: Parts of 17 listed in 16

definitions.meaning: the blades a sled slides on
the horses entered in a race appear on the printed programme

explanation.walkthrough: 17 is TOBOGGAN, which slides on blades of this name; 16 is RACECARD, which lists the horses taking part.
explanation.definitionFit: A sled rides on long blades, and the horses entered in a race share that name.

clue.text: In road repair a small volume of harmony

indicators.note: in says one piece goes inside the other
repair says the letters of road are mended into a new order

parts.note: cc is a cubic centimetre, a small volume

explanation.surface: Roadworks are done with a little volume of agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repair' rearranges ROAD to AORD, with CC put in.
explanation.definitionFit: Agreement between parties is harmony between them.

clue.text: Shaw playfully asserts William Archer's incompetence

definitions.text: Shaw playfully asserts William Archer's incompetence

parts.words: Shaw playfully asserts William Archer's incompetence
parts.note: the title of a comedy by Shaw, read as a statement that William, the archer Tell, cannot do something

explanation.walkthrough: William Archer looks like the drama critic of that name, a friend of Shaw's, but here it is William Tell the archer; the play's title, read as a sentence, says Tell can't.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's comedy has this title, and read word for word it says the Swiss bowman is unable.

clue.text: Poet's quondam address to girls in khaki

parts.note: ye is a former, archaic word for 'you'
the ATS, the Auxiliary Territorial Service, was the British women's army in khaki during the war

explanation.surface: A poet once greeted servicewomen in uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: The ATS was the women's branch of the British army in the Second World War; quondam means former.
explanation.definitionFit: W.B. Yeats was the Irish poet who won the Nobel Prize.

clue.text: Repealed law to be precise

parts.note: ex means former, as a repealed law is
an act is a law passed by parliament

explanation.surface: A statute is struck off to make things accurate.
explanation.definitionFit: Exact means accurate or correct in every detail.

clue.text: Lone wolf by the Waingunga

parts.note: in Kipling's Jungle Book the Waingunga is the river beside which the wolf pack lives, led by the Lone Wolf

explanation.walkthrough: In Kipling's Jungle Book the leader of the Seeonee wolf pack, near the Waingunga river, is called the Lone Wolf; his name was later used for Cub Scout leaders.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's pack leader in the Jungle Book is the big grey Lone Wolf who lives by that Indian river.

clue.text: Note for note reputed to be as previously mentioned

parts.note: A is a musical note
E is another musical note
something reputed is said to be so

explanation.surface: A rumour is passed on note by note, just as was stated earlier.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal-sounding word meaning named or stated earlier in the same document.

clue.text: Temporarily or permanently deprived of functions ?

definitions.text: Temporarily or permanently deprived of functions ?

parts.words: Temporarily or permanently deprived of functions
parts.note: an official can be barred from duties for a while; a hanged man, hung up by the neck, loses all functions for good

explanation.walkthrough: The temporary sense is a suspension from a job; the permanent one is hanging, being hung from a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: Barred from duty for a period, or hung from a gallows, both leave one without functions.

clue.text: 8.40 was time enough for this Dickensian house

definitions.text: 8.40 was time enough for this Dickensian house

parts.words: 8.40 was time enough for this Dickensian house
parts.note: in Great Expectations Miss Havisham stopped all the clocks of her house at twenty to nine; the house's Latin name means 'enough'

explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's Great Expectations Miss Havisham's house has every clock stopped at twenty to nine, and its Latin name means 'enough', so the time there was always enough.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss Havisham's home in Great Expectations bears a Latin name meaning sufficient, and its clocks halted at twenty to nine.
